title: Dolls House
strapline: A tiny home for big feelings — bedtime, breakfast and everything families do, replayed in miniature.
intent: Give children a safe, small stage to replay home life — bedtime, breakfast, bathtime, visitors — and make sense of it from the outside.
Process feelings and changes at one remove: a new baby, a house move or a wobbly goodbye is easier to explore when it happens to a doll.
Talk about families as they really are — children's own, and families that look different — with warmth and genuine interest.
Build room-by-room spatial language: upstairs and downstairs, next to the window, behind the sofa, under the little bed.
Grow cooperative pretend play with negotiated roles: someone must be the dad, and someone must agree to it.
implementation: Keep the doll families deliberately varied — different skin tones, generations and family shapes — so every child can find their family, and meet others.
Play alongside at the children's pace, taking a doll and following their storyline rather than steering it.
Give the house a daily rhythm that mirrors the children's own: wake up, breakfast, nursery drop-off, tea, bath, story, bed.
Listen more than you talk — the dolls house is where children rehearse home, and their play tells you what matters to them right now.
Feed in feeling words through the dolls: 'this little one looks worried about the first day — what would help?'
Model positional talk as furniture moves: 'so the cot goes next to the big bed, and the lamp behind it'.
Reflect real events children mention — a new baby, moving house, grandparents visiting — by quietly adding the right props.
key_questions: Who lives in this house, and who is coming to visit today?
What does this family do first when they wake up?
How is this doll feeling tonight — and what would help?
Where should the new baby sleep — and why there?
What's the same about this family and yours? What's different?

impact.text: Children replay home routines in careful detail — cooking breakfast, running the bath, tucking each doll in with a story.
Children give the dolls feelings and name them — this one is sad, that one is cross about bedtime — and find the doll something that helps.
Children direct and narrate the household — 'you be the dad, he's making tea, the baby's crying again' — keeping the story running through talk.
Children arrange furniture using positional language — the cot next to the big bed, the table under the window, shoes behind the door.
Children match and sort the household — chairs to the kitchen, beds to the bedrooms, one cup for each doll at the table.
Children talk about their own families through the play and notice that other families are different — and interesting.
Children replay real events from their own lives — the new baby arriving, moving house, Grandma's visit — in rough sequence through the dolls.
Children run the household together, negotiating who plays whom and whose storyline the family follows next.

enhancements: A new-baby basket: a tiny cot, blanket and bottle, quietly added when a real sibling is on the way.
A removals day: a small cardboard van and boxes for packing the whole house up and moving it in again.
Fabric scraps, small boxes and dough for children to make the furniture the house is missing.
A 'visitors' basket of extra dolls — grandparents, friends, a health visitor — to knock at the door.
Photos of the children's own homes and families displayed beside the house for talk and comparison.
Miniature festival props — birthday cake, Eid lanterns, a Christmas tree, Diwali divas — reflecting the room's real celebrations.
A tiny pet (and its basket) with the responsibility that follows: someone must remember to feed it.

playing_exploring: Children step into every role a home holds — parent, baby, visitor — and try each one on for size.
Opening the house is opening a world: children explore room by room, deciding what belongs where.
active_learning: Children see whole routines through from waking the dolls to lights-out, holding the sequence themselves.
Setting the table for every doll — one plate, one cup, one chair each — is checked and re-checked until it's fair.
creating_thinking: Children rework real life into story, testing out how a worry ends differently when they are in charge of it.
Two children merging their storylines — whose bedtime, whose visitor — takes real flexible thinking.
